_meta.name: FlameGuard lessons learned from spacecraft fire incidents
_meta.integrity_rule: Facts come from the cited pages. Fields marked source_quality=secondary come from non-NASA pages and should be double-checked before putting them in the final report. Section 'design_takeaways' is OUR interpretation, not official NASA procedure.
_meta.warning: Educational research content. Not an operational fire-response procedure.

facts.fact: Fire swept the capsule in seconds, fed by about 70 lb of flammable material (nylon netting, Velcro) and pure oxygen.
Opening the hatch took at least 90 seconds, while the fire consumed the cabin oxygen in about 25 seconds.
Investigators concluded a spark in the electrical system was the likely ignition source; they could not pinpoint the exact spot.
Cabin pressure rose rapidly during the fire (reported from 16.7 psi to over 29 psi), which kept the inward-opening hatch sealed.

changes_made: Ground-test atmosphere changed from pure oxygen to a nitrogen/oxygen mix (NASA agreed on a 60/40 O2/N2 launch atmosphere on 1968-03-14).
Hatch redesigned to open outward for fast egress.
Flammable interior materials replaced with self-extinguishing alternatives; wiring and plumbing rerouted.
NASA safety culture changed: Senate review found many people failed to recognize a hazardous situation.

incidents.type: Electrically initiated fire inside an oxygen tank (not a cabin fire)

environment.microgravity_relevance: In transit to the Moon; tank fans were used to stir the oxygen.

facts.fact: Review board concluded an electrically initiated fire in oxygen tank 2 caused the accident.
Damaged Teflon insulation on wiring inside the tank shorted and ignited; the fire raised pressure until the tank burst (overpressure, not a chemical explosion).
Heater thermostat switches were welded closed during ground testing; the heater probably reached about 500 C (1,000 F) but the gauge only read up to 85 F, so crews did not notice.
Board recommended redesign of the oxygen storage system and minimizing combustible items inside the tank (done for Apollo 14).

incidents.note_for_team: Apollo 13 is an oxygen-fed fire in a closed tank, not a flame in the crew cabin. It still teaches the same rule as Apollo 1: oxygen-rich spaces plus damaged insulation plus a spark is dangerous.

incidents.type: Fire in orbit (microgravity) from a solid-fuel oxygen generator (Vika/SFOG candle)

facts.fact: A canister burst into flame, shooting a flame about three feet long with sparks and molten metal and producing dense smoke.
The flame blocked the path to the docked Soyuz escape vehicle.
The candle type had been used more than 2,500 times without incident.
Crew put on masks and fought the fire with foam extinguishers; the station life support cleared smoke over several hours.
Burning metal globules were thrown into microgravity and splattered on the opposite bulkhead.

changes_made: Russia changed crew emergency training and ground controller response.
Candle safety improved and a fire-resistant screen was developed; SFOG now used on ISS with extra safety measures.
ISS oxygen supply has dissimilar redundancy (Elektron units + US Oxygen Generation System) with SFOG as backup.

iss_fire_safety_hardware.item: CO2 extinguishers in US segment; water-based foam in Russian segment
Water mist portable extinguisher under development to replace Halon-type agents (Halon 1301 phased out due to the 1994 Montreal Protocol motivation)
Water mist project tested droplet size and water amount in ground and free-fall tests (2011-2016) for ISS scenarios: open cabin, rack, stored-energy O2 candle, elevated O2

microgravity_fire_science_links.link: No buoyancy: a candle flame is a small blue flame at the wick in space, not the tall yellow teardrop seen on Earth.
Airflow matters more than on Earth: in microgravity the fan controls how much oxygen reaches the flame. A flame can be sustained or quenched by ventilation speed.
Low flow can extinguish flames: ISS thin-solid test went out when flow dropped to 2.2 cm/s at 18.7% O2 (see flameguard_compact_seed.json, record M3).
More oxygen means easier burning: spread rate rose with O2 and flow up to about 22%, and quenching flow speed fell as O2 rose.

design_takeaways.label: OUR interpretation of the sources above. Not official NASA procedure.

items.takeaway: Control the oxygen fraction and total pressure of the cabin; every incident above involved an oxygen-rich environment.
Reduce combustible materials and test them at the worst-case O2 and pressure, not only at normal air.
Protect wiring insulation and monitor heaters/electrics with instruments that read beyond normal range.
Cutting ventilation can quench a flame (BASS B1, ISS thin-solid test) but does NOT help when the fire has its own oxygen source, like an oxygen candle. Treat it as one tool, not a rule.
Keep escape routes clear of hazardous equipment and ensure quick egress; Mir's flame blocked the Soyuz route.
Use personal protection (masks) and the right extinguisher agent for the segment; train crews and ground teams together.
Treat Earth-based flammability results with caution; microgravity changes flame shape and flow dependence.
